analysis.one_liner: Guarantees emergency care and direct specialist access in employer health plans and creates small-business association plans.
analysis.headline: Introduced by a single House member with zero cosponsors, the bill never left committee and died when the 106th Congress ended without ever reaching a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the federal law governing most employer health plans. Patients would get a set of protections: doctors could not be gagged from advising them, emergency rooms would be covered by a 'prudent layperson' standard without pre-approval, women could see an OB/GYN and parents could pick a pediatrician directly, plans would have to disclose coverage details and drug formulary changes, and denied claims would face strict deadlines for internal review plus optional review by an independent outside medical expert. It would also create a new federally certified framework letting small businesses buy coverage together through association health plans, and it would make these federal review procedures the exclusive route for patients, overriding state-law remedies.
analysis.who_benefits: People covered by employer group health plans — particularly women who want direct OB/GYN access, parents of children needing pediatric specialists, patients needing emergency care, and anyone whose coverage claim gets denied and wants a faster, medically informed appeal. Small business owners and their employees would also gain a new route to pooled coverage through association health plans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and families in employer health plans

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits plans from restricting what health professionals can tell patients about their condition or treatment options, including care the plan does not cover.
Requires plans that cover emergency care to pay for emergency screening without pre-authorization or network limits whenever a prudent layperson would consider it necessary.
Lets women get routine obstetric and gynecological care from a specialist without a primary care referral, and lets parents designate a pediatric specialist as their child's primary care provider.

Requires plans to disclose covered and excluded benefits, cost-sharing, drug formulary rules, and referral limits, and to give 30 days' notice before removing a drug used to treat a chronic illness from the formulary.

Sets deadlines for coverage decisions (30 days normally, 5 days for urgent accelerated-need care), requires review of medical-necessity denials by medical professionals, and creates an optional external review by independent medical experts for certain denied claims.
Establishes certification, solvency, and enforcement rules for association health plans through which small businesses and trade associations can offer coverage to their members.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and health insurers would bear the cost of complying with the coverage, disclosure, and appeal requirements. Patients would also pay in a less visible way: the bill makes the federal review process the exclusive remedy and preempts state law, so participants would generally lose the ability to challenge denied claims in state court, and external review is elective — plans can offer alternative procedures in which the patient waives further review, with the patient potentially owing a small advance payment (capped around $100).
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, insurers, and patients' legal remedies

drawbacks.text: The bill makes the federal claim and review procedures 'the exclusive procedures and remedies' and supersedes state-law review or causes of action, meaning patients in ERISA plans would generally not be able to sue in state court over denied care.

External review is elective rather than mandatory, is available only for decisions involving medical necessity, investigational items, or experimental treatment (not eligibility, dollar limits, or copay rules), and plans may substitute alternative review procedures in which the patient waives the right to judicial review in advance.
The patient seeking external review may have to make an advance payment of up to the lesser of $100 or 10 percent of the cost of care (with low-income Medicaid and CHIP participants exempt).

No enforcement action or penalty applies before final regulations are issued if the plan acts in good faith, and the new rights phase in a year or more after enactment, with collectively bargained plans delayed until at least January 1, 2002.

The external reviewer's decision is made the final decision of the plan, and a regular review decision that modifies the initial denial must find the record sufficient to 'rebut a presumption in favor of the decision below,' tilting the default toward the plan's original ruling.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient-facing protections are real and concrete — a gag-clause ban, a prudent-layperson emergency standard, direct OB/GYN and pediatric access, honest disclosure, and appeal deadlines are things ordinary plan members would feel. But the bill is deliberately weighted toward plan sponsors: remedies are channeled into a federal review process that preempts state court, external review is optional and narrow, deadlines favor the plan's original decision, and compliance is penalty-free until regulations issue. It was written as a managed-care-friendly alternative to stronger patient-protection proposals of the era, and the trade — real rights in exchange for giving up state-law remedies — reflects that. A fair assessment: meaningful gains for patients, purchased at the cost of weaker legal recourse.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. John Boehner introduced the Health Care Quality and Access Act of 1999 on June 9, 1999, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
Two days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where the committee record for the bill ends.
The bill drew no cosponsors from either party.
No further action was taken in the House, and the bill received no floor vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so every stakeholder kept the existing rules: employer plans and insurers faced no new coverage mandates, while patients got no new rights from this bill. Because the bill also would have preempted state lawsuits and softened remedies, its death left patients no worse off on that front, but the proposed patient protections — emergency care standards, direct specialist access, appeal deadlines — never took effect either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employer plans and insurers kept the status quo

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral (chairmanship not identified in the record)
against.what_they_did: After receiving the referral on June 9, 1999 and forwarding it to the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee, never held a hearing or markup or reported the bill, letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan roll-call record exists.

industries.note: Insurers would take on new coverage, disclosure, and appeal obligations with no penalties until regulations issue, but they would also gain a key protection: the bill makes the federal review process exclusive and preempts state-law claims, narrowing patients' ability to sue. Patients would gain new rights while losing some legal recourse.

Employers would bear compliance costs for the new patient rights, but as plan sponsors they would benefit most from the federal preemption of state court remedies over denied care — a gain that comes directly out of patients' legal options.

industries.industry: Trade and professional associations offering health coverage
industries.note: The bill builds a full federal certification and solvency framework for association health plans, opening a new channel for small businesses and trade groups to pool coverage. It could lower premiums for members of small firms, but pooling across state lines tends to weaken state insurance oversight and consumer protections.
A ban on gag clauses and mandatory review of medical-necessity denials by medical professionals strengthens clinicians' standing against plan administrators, an interest that runs with patients'.
